Description: explicit — client-side hypsometric tint (color-relief layer, GL JS 5.6+)
prompt: I have terrain tiles as a raster-dem source in MapLibre GL JS and I want to color the map by elevation ranges (a hypsometric tint) directly client-side — blues at sea level through greens and browns to white peaks — without pre-rendering colored raster tiles. What layer type do I use and how do I configure the color ramp?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** *Use a **`color-relief`** layer.* It reads the same `raster-dem` source you already have and lets you paint the DEM directly with an **`interpolate` expression on the `["elevation"]` expression**. The ramp you write inside the `color-relief-color` paint property is the hypsometric tint (blue → green → brown → white). Below is a complete, copy-and-paste-ready example that shows: 1. Adding the DEM source (if you haven’t already). 2. Adding a `color-relief` layer that colors the terrain by elevation. 3. Optional tweaks (opacity, resampling, exaggeration, camera pitch). --- ## 1. DEM source (raster-dem) ```json { "id": "terrain-dem", "type": "raster-dem", "url": "https://my.tileserver.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", "tileSize": 256, "maxzoom": 14, "encoding": "terrarium" // or "mapbox" – must match the tiles you serve } ``` Add it to the map (JS): ```js map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://my.tileserver.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png', tileSize: 256, maxzoom: 14, encoding: 'terrarium' // adjust to your DEM encoding }); ``` > **Note** – The source is *only* a `raster-dem`. Do **not** add a `raster` layer for it; the `color-relief` layer will read the elevation values directly. --- ## 2. `color-relief` layer – hypsometric tint ```json { "id": "hypsometric-tint", "type": "color-relief", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "color-relief-color": [ "interpolate", ["linear"], // smooth linear ramp ["elevation"], // elevation in metres (from the DEM) /* ---- elevation (m) → colour ---- */ 0, "#2c7bb6", // deep ocean – dark blue 50, "#3b8cc4", // shallow water – lighter blue 200, "#73c0e5", // near-shore – cyan 500, "#a8ddb5", // lowland – light green 1000, "#c7e9b4", // foothills – greener 1500, "#e6f5c9", // mid-elevation – yellow-green 2000, "#fee08b", // sub-alpine – light yellow 2500, "#fdae61", // alpine – orange 3000, "#f46d43", // high alpine – reddish-orange 3500, "#d53e4f", // near-summit – dark red 4000, "#ffffff" // snow-capped peaks – white ], "color-relief-opacity": 0.85, // optional – make it a little translucent "resampling": "linear" // optional – GL JS ≥ 5.20, choose "nearest" or "linear" } } ``` ### How the ramp works * The **first element** of the array is the expression type (`"interpolate"`). * The **second element** is the interpolation method (`"linear"` is the most common; `"exponential"` is also allowed). * The **third element** is the input expression – here `["elevation"]`, which returns the elevation (in metres) for the current pixel of the DEM. * The remaining pairs are **stop-value → colour**. * You can add as many stops as you like; the more stops you add, the smoother the colour transition. * The values are **absolute metres** (not “meters above sea level” unless your DEM is already referenced to sea level). > **Tip:** If you want a “hard” contour-like step instead of a smooth gradient, replace `"linear"` with `"step"` and give a colour for each threshold. --- ## 3. (Optional) Show the terrain in 3-D If you also want to see the surface in true 3-D (extruded mesh) you can enable terrain **and** keep the `color-relief` layer underneath any other layers you want to drape over it. ```js // Enable the mesh (the DEM source must already be added) map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain-dem', exaggeration: 1.0 // increase >1.0 to exaggerate relief }); // Tilt the camera so the relief becomes visible map.easeTo({ pitch: 60, bearing: 0, duration: 2000 }); ``` > **Important:** The `color-relief` layer works **independently** of `setTerrain`. You can have a `color-relief` layer *without* any 3-D terrain (flat map) or *with* terrain (3-D view). The layer always paints the DEM values directly. --- ## 4. Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre – Hypsometric Tint (color-relief)
``` --- ## 5. Quick checklist | ✅ | What you need | |---|----------------| | **Layer type** | `type: "color-relief"` | | **Source** | A `raster-dem` source (the same one you use for `setTerrain` or hillshade). | | **Paint property** | `color-relief-color` with an `interpolate` (or `step`) expression that uses `["elevation"]`. | | **Optional paint** | `color-relief-opacity` (0-1), `resampling` (`"linear"` or `"nearest"`). | | **Version** | MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.6 (the `color-relief` layer was introduced in 5.6). | | **No pre-rendered tiles** | The raster-DEM is decoded client-side; the color ramp is applied on-the-fly. | | **If you also want 3-D** | Call `map.setTerrain({source:'terrain-dem', exaggeration:…})` and pitch the map. | --- ### TL;DR ```json { "id": "hypsometric-tint", "type": "color-relief", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "color-relief-color": [ "interpolate", ["linear"], ["elevation"], 0, "#2c7bb6", 200, "#abd9e9", 500, "#a8ddb5", 1500,"#ffffbf", 2500,"#fdae61", 4000,"#ffffff" ], "color-relief-opacity": 0.9 } } ``` That’s all you need to get a client-side hypsometric tint on a `raster-dem` source in MapLibre GL JS. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh”

A **single** `hillshade` layer already gives you everything you need to tone the relief.  
Harshness usually comes from one (or a combination) of these paint properties:

| Property | What it does | Typical harsh-looking value |
|----------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| `hillshade-method` | How the light is computed. `standard` (default) uses a single light source, which can produce very dark shadows and very bright highlights. | `standard` |
| `hillshade-exaggeration` | Multiplies the slope before shading. Values > 0.5 make shadows/ highlights pop. | `0.7-1.0` |
| `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Azimuth of the light (0-360°). Certain angles line up with map features and make the contrast look “blown out”. | `335°` (default) |
| `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Where the light is anchored. `viewport` keeps the light fixed to the screen; `map` makes it rotate with the map bearing. | `viewport` |
| `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Pure black / pure white give maximum contrast. | `#000000` / `#FFFFFF` |

If any of those are left at the defaults (or you have manually set a high `exaggeration`), the result will be a black-and-white, “chalky” relief.

---

## Quick Fixes (pick the ones you need)

### 1. Switch to a softer shading **method**
```json
{
  "id": "hillshade",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",
  "paint": {
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",   // or "igor"
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4,            // lower than the default 0.5-0.6
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map",   // light rotates with the map (optional)
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"
  }
}
```
* **`multidirectional`** lights the surface from several directions in a *single* pass, giving a much softer, more natural look.  
* **`igor`** is another soft option that tries to keep the underlying map features visible.

### 2. Reduce the contrast with alpha-blended colors
```json
"hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.45)",          // 45 % opacity instead of solid black
"hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,255,255,0.35)" // 35 % opacity instead of solid white
```
Adding opacity lets the underlying imagery show through and removes the “black-and-white” feel.

### 3. Lower the exaggeration (optional)
```json
"hillshade-exaggeration": 0.3   // 0-1 range, 0.5 is the default
```
A smaller exaggeration flattens the slope before shading, which directly reduces shadow depth.

### 4. Tweak the illumination direction (optional)
If the light is coming from a direction that aligns with a dominant ridge/valley, the contrast can look extreme. Try a different azimuth:
```json
"hillshade-illumination-direction": 225   // southwest light, for example
```
You can experiment with any value 0-360° until the terrain feels natural.

### 5. Anchor the light to the map (optional)
```json
"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"
```
When the map is rotated, the light rotates with it, preventing a “fixed-to-screen” glare that can look harsh at certain bearings.

---

## Full Example – One-layer, soft hillshade

```javascript
// Assuming you already have a raster-dem source called "terrain-dem"
map.addLayer({
  id: "soft-hillshade",
  type: "hillshade",
  source: "terrain-dem",
  paint: {
    // 1️⃣ Soft method
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",

    // 2️⃣ Light contrast with opacity
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)",

    // 3️⃣ Slightly lower exaggeration
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4,

    // 4️⃣ Optional direction & anchor tweaks
    "hillshade-illumination-direction": 225,
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"
  }
});
```

**Result:** A single hillshade layer that looks smooth, warm-shadowed, and integrates nicely with any basemap or overlay.

---

## What **NOT** to do

* **Don’t stack multiple hillshade layers** to simulate multi-directional lighting. Since GL JS 5.5 the `hillshade-method` does that in one pass; stacking just adds extra draw calls and can make the contrast even harsher.
* **Don’t use `raster` layers** for a DEM if you want shading – a `raster` layer will just display the raw RGB-encoded elevation tiles, not a shaded relief.
* **Don’t try Mapbox-only properties** (`setFog`, `sky-type`, etc.) – they are not part of MapLibre and will be ignored.

---

## TL;DR Checklist

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| ✅ | Set `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` (or `"igor"`). |
| ✅ | Give `hillshade-shadow-color` and `hillshade-highlight-color` an alpha value (e.g., `rgba(...,0.4)`). |
| ✅ | Lower `"hillshade-exaggeration"` to ~0.3-0.4. |
| ✅ | (Optional) Change `"hillshade-illumination-direction"` and/or `"hillshade-illumination-anchor"` to suit your map orientation. |
| ✅ | Keep it to **one** hillshade layer – no stacking. |

Apply the snippet above, tweak the numbers to your taste, and the harsh black-and-white look should disappear. Happy mapping!
